Backpressure is a mechanism in streaming pipelines that allows slow downstream consumers to communicate upstream to a faster producer, requesting that the producer reduce or pace its emission rate. Without backpressure, a mismatch in processing speed between producer and consumer can cause an unbounded buffer to grow, ultimately exhausting system memory.

## Purpose

In any data pipeline where a producer generates data faster than a consumer can process it, backpressure prevents memory overflow by:
- Coupling the production rate to the consumption rate
- Avoiding the accumulation of unprocessed items in memory
- Maintaining stable resource usage across the system

## Common Implementations

The source identifies three major approaches to implementing backpressure:

### Bounded Queue / Blocking Producer
The producer writes items to a bounded queue. Once the queue reaches capacity, further writes block until the consumer drains items from the queue. This synchronous blocking approach is simple and provides automatic backpressure without explicit signaling.

### Credit-Based Flow Control
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a fixed number of items (the "credit"). The producer may only emit up to its current credit balance; as the credit is consumed, the consumer replenishes it. This decouples producer and consumer timing while maintaining control over emission rates.

### Reactive-Pull Model
Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer pulls items on its own schedule. The producer only generates items when the consumer requests them, eliminating the need for a separate backpressure signal—demand itself is the signal. This is the approach used in reactive streams libraries.
